power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Correlation-Based, Parameter-Based, or Fixed-Effect? A Comparison of One-Stage Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling Approaches

author.affiliation: Leibniz Institute for Science and Mathematics Education Kiel
Leibniz Institute for Science and Mathematics Education Kiel
Leibniz Institute for Science and Mathematics Education Kiel

text.text: Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) is increasingly used in psychological research to evaluate multivariate models, such as path or factor models, across multiple primary studies.

Several approaches to MASEM have been proposed that differ in whether and where they represent between-study heterogeneity, most notably the fixed-effect, correlation-based, and parameter-based approaches.
This study investigates under which conditions these approaches target equivalent or divergent structural parameter estimates.
We derive analytical conditions for equivalence and divergence and examine them in three simulation studies comparing one-stage implementations under parameter-based data-generating mechanisms.
The results show that the approaches produce approximately equivalent estimates when the model-implied correlations depend linearly on the heterogeneous parameters.
However, multidimensional, correlated parameter heterogeneity produces target discrepancies between the parameter-based and the other two approaches.
These discrepancies increase with the magnitude of between-study heterogeneity.
Nonlinear parameter transformations introduce additional discrepancies, even under unidimensional heterogeneity.
Under the standard implementations used, almost no differences emerged between the fixed-effect and the correlation-based population targets.
Two applications to psychological research further illustrate the model comparison.

Overall, the findings show that the location of random effects can affect the target of structural parameter estimation in MASEM even when the study-specific structural models are correctly specified.

It follows that the choice among the approaches constitutes a substantive decision for researchers between distinct statistical estimands: the mean of study-specific structural parameters (parameter-based MASEM) and a common parameter vector that best represents the mean correlations across studies (fixed-effect and correlation-based MASEM).

Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) combines the statistical approaches of meta-analysis and structural equation modeling (SEM) to evaluate multivariate theoretical models across multiple primary studies (e.g., Cheung, 2015a).

text.text: It has become an increasingly popular tool in psychological research for synthesizing findings on multivariate interrelations, with research applications mainly focusing on the evaluation of path models testing multivariate psychological theories (e.g., Hagger et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Möller et al., 2020; Scherer et al., 2019; Vasconcellos et al., 2025), as well as the examination of latent factor structures across studies (e.g., Gnambs & Staufenbiel, 2018; Kindred et al., 2026; Koğar & Koğar, 2024; Naragon-Gainey et al., 2017; Schroeders et al., 2022; Strunk et al., 2021; Yeung et al., 2020).

text.text: In psychological research, primary studies addressing the same theoretical model or research question are rarely exact replications.
They typically differ in sample characteristics, measurement instruments, operationalizations, and study designs.
As a consequence, substantial between-study heterogeneity beyond sampling error is typically found in meta-analyses (e.g., Hunter & Schmidt, 2004).

text.text: In psychological research, meta-analytic methods are therefore essential not only for aggregating findings but also for examining the generalizability of theoretical models and identifying conditions under which they hold or do not hold (Hunter & Schmidt, 2004; Schmidt, 2015).

The remainder of this article is organized as follows.
We first introduce the fixed-effect, correlation-based, and parameter-based approaches to MASEM.

Building on their statistical formulations, we derive conditions under which the approaches can be expected to yield asymptotically equivalent SEM parameter estimates and conditions under which their targets may diverge.
We then examine these expectations in three simulation studies-using both path models and confirmatory factor analysis models-in which the data-generating process follows a parameter-based model.
Next, we illustrate differences among the approaches using two empirical examples from psychological research.
Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings and directions for future research.

text.text: However, the structural parameters themselves have received surprisingly little attention so far, even though the three approaches target distinct statistical estimands.

The parameter-based approach estimates the mean of the study-specific structural parameters and thus addresses the research question: What are the average structural parameters across the population of studies?
The fixed-effect and correlation-based approaches instead estimate the structural parameters that best reproduce the marginal mean correlation structure and thus address the research question:
What single set of structural parameters best accounts for the average pattern of correlations across studies?

In addition, although the fixed-effect and correlation-based approaches address the same question, they may arrive at different answers because they weight the study-specific contributions differently (Forte & Tipton, 2026; Hafdahl, 2008).

Because averaging structural parameters and parameterizing the average correlation structure need not yield the same result, these questions can have different answers even when the study-specific structural models are correctly specified.
The central question addressed in the current article is under which conditions the answers coincide and under which conditions they diverge.

We now examine conditions under which the three approaches, although targeting different statistical estimands, converge to the same structural parameter vector and conditions under which their targets may diverge.
In the present analyses, we use a parameter-based data-generating mechanism as the reference setting to study the consequences of locating heterogeneity at different levels.
This choice serves as an analytical device and does not imply that parameter-based MASEM is generally preferable or that heterogeneity necessarily originates at the parameter level.
Our examination is conducted under the following conditions.
First, it is assumed that the same structural model is correctly specified within every primary study, so that each study-specific population correlation vector equals ρ(θ s ).

The analysis therefore does not concern structural model misspecification within primary studies but focuses on discrepancies that may arise when-instead of averaging structural parameters across correctly specified study-specific models (parameter-based approach)-the average correlation structure is represented through a common structural parameter vector (fixed-effect and correlation-based approach).
Second, primary studies are independent, sampling errors are unbiased, and there are no systematic associations of sample size with the study-specific structural parameters.
Furthermore, all results in the current section concern the asymptotic structural parameter targets of the three MASEM approaches as the number of primary studies tends to infinity.

The preceding analysis showed how the asymptotic targets of the parameter-based approach and the common-parameter approaches (i.e., fixed-effect and correlation-based MASEM) may diverge under parameter-based data generation.

Curvature in the mapping from structural parameters to model-implied correlations can produce a mean-correlation discrepancy that grows with the magnitude of parameter heterogeneity and that translates into structural parameter target differences through the local sensitivity of the model.
These mechanisms yield several qualitative predictions that the following simulation studies are designed to examine.
First, correlated, multidimensional parameter heterogeneity should produce target discrepancies even in conventional structural models, whereas unidimensional heterogeneity need not.
Second, nonlinear parameter transformations should introduce additional discrepancies and show discrepancies even under unidimensional heterogeneity.
Third, target discrepancies between the parameter-based approach and the fixed-effect and correlation-based approaches should increase with the magnitude of parameter heterogeneity.
Finally, because these predictions concern asymptotic targets, the corresponding discrepancies should persist as the number of primary studies increases.

Another potential source of target discrepancies between the fixed-effect and the correlation-based approaches concerns overidentified models.

In such models, the marginal mean correlation vector may not be reproducible by a single structural parameter vector, because the model-implied correlations occupy a lower-dimensional space than m ρ .

The model was just identified, with six unique correlations and six structural parameters.

Accordingly, the mean structural parameter vector θ PB contained four regression coefficients-in the following referred to as β 11,PB , β 22,PB , β 12,PB , β 21,PB -, the correlation between the two predictors ϕ x,PB , and the residual covariance between the two outcomes ψ PB .
The mean regression coefficients were set to β 11,PB = 0.40, β 22,PB = 0.30, β 12,PB = 0.20, and β 21,PB = 0.10.
The mean predictor correlation was set to ϕ PB = 0.30, and the mean residual covariance was set to ψ PB = 0.15.
We systematically varied three design factors.

First, the random-effects structure comprised a single-random-effect condition, in which only the residual covariance ψ s varied across studies, and a full-random-effects condition, in which all six structural parameters varied across studies.
In the latter condition, T θ was a 6 × 6 covariance matrix.
Second, we varied the magnitude of heterogeneity by setting the random-effect standard deviations (RE SD ) to either 0.05 or 0.10.

In the full-random-effects condition, the off-diagonal elements of the random-effects correlation matrix were drawn from a uniform distribution ranging from 0.20 to 0.70, subject to the resulting matrix being positive definite.
The resulting correlation matrix was held constant across Monte Carlo replications.
Third, the number of primary studies was varied across conditions and set to S = 20, 50, 100, or 500.
The three design factors were fully crossed, resulting in 2 × 2 ×4 = 16 simulation conditions.

In the data generation, for each primary study s, the study-specific structural parameter vector θ s was generated from the parameter-based random-effects distribution and substituted into the path model to obtain the study-specific population correlation matrix R s , with ρ(θ s ) = vechs(R s ).

The study-specific sample size n s was drawn from a truncated lognormal distribution with a lower bound of 200, where the logarithm of the values was normally distributed with mean 5.75 and standard deviation 0.50.

Taken together, the three simulation studies supported the theoretical expectation that the location of the random effects in MASEM approaches can affect the asymptotic targets of structural parameters, even in relatively simple path models and CFA models, such as those frequently used in MASEM studies.

Across all three studies, moving from a single random effect to multidimensional, correlated parameter heterogeneity either introduced or amplified persistent deviations of the fixed-effect and correlation-based estimates from the parameter-based reference values.
These deviations were generally larger under stronger heterogeneity.

This pattern is consistent with the order-of-averaging argument presented above: When several structural parameters vary jointly across studies, products and cross-products of these parameters can result in a marginal mean correlation vector that differs from the correlation vector implied by the average model parameters across studies.
Importantly, this occurred even though the study-specific structural models were correctly specified and are conventionally classified as linear SEMs.
Across all three studies, the Taylor approximations provided accurate predictions of the observed target discrepancies between the parameter-based and the common-parameter approaches.
In Simulation Studies 1 and 2, predicted and observed values agreed to three decimal places for most parameters.

In Simulation Study 3, the predictions remained qualitatively accurate but showed somewhat larger deviations from the observed values under RE SD = 0.10, which is likely due to the contribution of higher-order terms not captured by the second-order Taylor approximation.
Nevertheless, the approximations correctly predicted the relative magnitude, direction, and scaling of the discrepancies across all conditions.

Comparing Simulation Studies 1 and 2 shows that both just-identified and overidentified structural models can produce discrepancies between the parameter-based and common-parameter targets when multidimensional, correlated heterogeneity is present.

In both studies, the single-random-effect conditions produced negligible discrepancies because the heterogeneous parameter entered the model-implied correlations linearly, eliminating the curvature required for a mean-correlation discrepancy.
The comparison between Simulation Studies 2 and 3 illustrates the additional consequences of nonlinear parameter transformations.

When the factor correlation varied on the Fisher z scale rather than the original scale, persistent discrepancies emerged even under unidimensional heterogeneity-confirming that nonlinear transformations can be a sufficient source of curvature.

Under multidimensional heterogeneity, the inverse-logit transformation of the loadings produced substantially larger discrepancies than those observed in Simulation Study 2, particularly for parameters with greater curvature in the transformation function.
Furthermore, varying the number of primary studies helped distinguish finite-sample effects from persistent target discrepancies.

Deviations of the parameter-based estimates in the more complex conditions of Simulation Study 3 largely disappeared as S increased, whereas several deviations of the fixed-effect and correlation-based estimates remained at S = 500.
This persistence is consistent with the fixed-effect and correlation-based approaches converging to targets that differ from the parameter-based reference, rather than with finite-sample bias alone.
Differences between the fixed-effect and correlation-based approaches were generally small across all three simulation studies.
In Simulation Studies 1 and 2, the two approaches produced virtually identical deviations at S = 500.
In Simulation Study 3, small but persistent differences emerged under full random effects, with the largest paired differences reaching approximately 0.002 at S = 500.
These differences were much smaller than those between the parameter-based and common-parameter approaches but were considerably different from zero based on their Monte Carlo standard errors.

The projection mechanism described in Section 1.2.5 offers one possible explanation: when the mean-correlation discrepancy cannot be exactly reproduced by a single parameter vector, approach-specific weighting may lead to slightly different approximations of the marginal mean vector.
However, the present simulation design was not specifically constructed to isolate this mechanism, and further research is needed in this respect.

In this study, we compared the correlation-based, parameter-based, and fixed-effect approaches to MASEM with respect to their approach-specific population estimands.
Our theoretical derivations showed that the three approaches can target systematically different quantities in common MASEM applications, including meta-analytic path models and CFAs.
In particular, the derivations identified the joint heterogeneity of multiple SEM parameters and covariance among their random effects as one mechanism that can produce target differences.

Consistent with this mechanism and bias predictions based on the second-order Taylor approximation, persistent differences emerged in simulation conditions that combined multidimensional heterogeneity with correlated random effects and generally increased with the magnitude of heterogeneity.
Moreover, nonlinear parameter transformations, which are commonly used to keep parameters within their admissible ranges, produced target differences even under unidimensional heterogeneity.
The magnitude of these differences depended on the heterogeneity and the local curvature of the transformation.
Across all simulation studies, the fixed-effect and correlation-based approaches produced largely equivalent results.

Small but statistically distinguishable differences between the two emerged only in Simulation Study 3 under the combination of nonlinear transformations, overidentification, and strong multidimensional heterogeneity, and even in this case they were considerably smaller than the discrepancies relative to the parameter-based approach.
However, the present simulation studies were not designed to systematically isolate the mechanisms driving differences between the fixed-effect and correlation-based approaches.
The two empirical examples further illustrated that the choice of MASEM approach can affect the resulting structural parameter estimates.
Although the estimates were generally similar, small differences emerged for individual path coefficients, item loadings, and latent factor correlations.
However, neither our theoretical considerations nor the simulation studies and empirical examples establish which approach is generally most appropriate.

Instead, the choice depends on the substantive estimand: Is the primary aim to estimate the SEM parameter vector that reproduces-or best approximates-the mean correlation structure across primary studies, or to investigate the mean and variance of the distribution of study-specific SEM parameters?
The estimand of a MASEM application should therefore be defined explicitly before selecting an analytic approach.
The parameter-based approach may be particularly suitable when researchers are interested in the average and the heterogeneity of SEM parameters across primary studies.

It also permits the calculation of prediction intervals for SEM parameters in a new study and extends naturally to moderator analyses, including the quantification of explained parameter heterogeneity (see Ke et al., 2025).

text.text: The correlation-based approach may be preferred when the mean correlation structure across primary studies is of central substantive interest and constitutes the starting point of the meta-analytic investigation.
By contrast, fixed-effect MASEM assumes that between-study variation beyond sampling error can be ignored.
This assumption may be implausible in many psychological applications and can lead to uncertainty estimates that are too small, as was also suggested by our empirical examples.

Nevertheless, it can provide a useful working model and may be combined with cluster-robust uncertainty-estimation, such as resampling, to support valid inference under between-study heterogeneity (Lohmann et al., 2026a).

text.text: Our findings should be considered in light of several limitations that also provide directions for future research.
First, an important issue concerns the dimensionality and specification of the random-effects covariance structure.

text.text: The number of heterogeneity variances and covariances in the correlation-based approach therefore increases considerably faster than the number of random-effects parameters in a parameter-based CFA.
Nevertheless, an unstructured random-effects covariance matrix can also become difficult to estimate in parameter-based MASEM, particularly when the number of primary studies is limited.

More parsimonious alternatives include estimating only a diagonal covariance matrix, imposing an equicorrelated structure with parameter-specific heterogeneity variances but a single common random-effects correlation (e.g., Jak & Cheung, 2026; Ke et al., 2019; Lohmann et al., 2026b), or regularizing the covariance parameters toward zero.
text.formatted: More parsimonious alternatives include estimating only a diagonal covariance matrix, imposing an equicorrelated structure with parameter-specific heterogeneity variances but a single common random-effects correlation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Jak & Cheung, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Ke et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Lohmann et al., 2026b)</ref>, or regularizing the covariance parameters toward zero.

text.text: Future research should compare the statistical and computational performance of these structures and examine their robustness when the assumed random-effects structure is misspecified.
Second, the simulations considered a limited set of data-generating conditions and assumed both a correctly specified structural model and normally distributed random effects.
Future studies could examine the consequences of model misspecification and skewed or otherwise nonnormal random-effects distributions.

Moreover, because the present data were generated from parameter-based models, complementary simulations could consider correlation-based data-generating mechanisms in which heterogeneity is introduced directly at the level of the correlations or hybrid mechanisms combining both sources of heterogeneity.

Third, the simulations did not directly manipulate conditions under which the weighting schemes of the fixed-effect and correlation-based approaches may result in different asymptotic targets for the structural parameters.

In particular, primary-study sample sizes were generated independently of the study-specific structural parameters (and correlations), potentially limiting weighting-dependent discrepancies (see, e.g., Forte & Tipton, 2026; Hafdahl, 2008).

text.text: Future research could examine informative-precision settings in which study size covaries with population correlations and thereby more directly isolate the interaction between weighting and model identification.
Finally, the two empirical examples provide only an initial indication of the differences that may arise in applied analyses.
Further comparisons across a broader range of real meta-analytic datasets and structural models are needed to assess the frequency and practical magnitude of approach-specific differences.

Our theoretical derivations, simulation studies, and empirical examples show that MASEM approaches can target different population quantities, depending on where between-study heterogeneity is represented in the model.

Differences between the parameter-based approach and the common-parameter approaches are particularly plausible under multidimensional, correlated heterogeneity or nonlinear parameter transformations and tend to increase with the magnitude of heterogeneity.

Researchers applying MASEM should consider whether their primary interest lies in a common SEM parameter vector representing the marginal correlation structure or in the mean of the study-specific SEM parameters.
